title: The Daughter Who Made Things
premise: At twenty-six, Frances Glessner Lee possesses an attorney husband, two children and an elegant townhouse her parents constructed. Her hands crave something different, and one block south her mother has just discovered it.

opening.text:
JAUNT: THE DAUGHTER WHO MADE THINGS. An overcast Monday morning, 21 November 1904, at the northern boundary of the Glessner family's domain.

Four stops, from the twin townhouses the Glessners constructed for their two children to the monumental stone residence at Eighteenth Street where the daughter was raised. Frances Glessner Lee is twenty-six, privately educated, married at nineteen, and the least probable person on this avenue to revolutionize the investigation of suspicious deaths. Attend carefully to her hands.

Begin at 1700 Prairie, at the entrance of the young Lees.

stops.text: 1700 Prairie, the northern half of a pair of twin townhouses that John and Frances Glessner commissioned for their two children, whose families took possession in 1902. This half belongs to their daughter Frances and her husband Blewett Lee, an attorney. Born in 1878, the youngest child and only daughter, she was "tutored at home" in the stone residence down the avenue and spent fourteen months touring Europe with her aunt before her debut. On 9 February 1898, at nineteen, she married Lee in her parents' drawing rooms, and the family's cook baked the wedding cake. There is now a son, John, aged six, and a daughter born the previous year. Observe the entrance: her husband departs for his office while she remains on the threshold. Her brother occupies the adjoining house.

stage.caption: Blewett Lee descends his steps and departs for his office, while his wife and their son remain at the entrance.

stops.text: 1706 Prairie, the other twin, sharing a party wall with the Lees. Here resides her brother George Glessner, his wife Alice and their four children, Elizabeth, Frances, John and the newborn Emily. George pursues photography with lifelong dedication; he documented these very houses under construction in 1901, and in 1902 he was appointed a utility manager at International Harvester. His existence is precisely what this avenue comprehends: a respectable position, an absorbing pastime, a crowded nursery. His sister's existence is expected to appear identical from the sidewalk, and superficially it does. Nevertheless her son would eventually attribute the disintegration of her marriage to her "creative urge coupled with high manual dexterity—the desire to make things—which [Lee] did not share". Walk one block south to discover that impulse's origin.

stage.caption: George and Alice Glessner emerge with their children for a morning promenade.

stops.text: 1800 Prairie, her childhood home, constructed with the defensive severity of a fortress at Eighteenth Street. Her mother, Frances Glessner, is fifty-six, and this year she has undertaken something few ladies of Prairie Avenue would contemplate. In 1904 she installed a workbench in the basement and began fabricating silver with her own hands, instructed by Annibale Fogliata, a master jewelry craftsman associated with Hull House, and by Madeline Yale Wynne, a distinguished Chicago silversmith. Every piece bears her hallmark, "a G encircling a honeybee", commemorating her beekeeping. She has maintained a meticulous journal since 1879, and virtually nothing escapes her observation. The daughter arrives at the entrance. Within is a mother who resolved, at fifty-six, to master a demanding manual discipline.

stage.caption: Frances Glessner Lee approaches her mother's entrance, and her mother opens the door herself.

stops.text: The courtyard, the sunlit and secluded center of the fortress. The mother displays what her hands have accomplished, and one can readily imagine what the daughter perceives: a woman of fifty-six who solicited nobody's permission, performing exacting, patient, beautiful work at a bench. Frances Glessner Lee is intelligent, restless and intellectually unfulfilled, and her marriage is "not a happy one". Her son would later identify the "creative urge coupled with high manual dexterity" that her husband never shared. Everything subsequent in her extraordinary life originates in what she observes at this moment: diminutive objects, fabricated with precision, by hand, inside a residence where every architectural detail operates as evidence. She will bear one more child. Then she will depart, and construct something nobody on this avenue could possibly have envisioned.

stage.caption: Mother and daughter stand together in the courtyard while the cook observes from the service entrance.

legs.story: Next door, through the party wall, to her brother's half of the twin townhouses.
South one block along Prairie Avenue to the stone residence at Eighteenth Street.
Through the residence to the courtyard, where the windows open generously.

endings.text: The walk concludes here. Martha was born in 1906, and in 1914 the Lees divorced. Decades afterward Frances Glessner Lee constructed the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death: miniature, scrupulously accurate interiors in which a death has occurred, executed at a scale of one inch to a foot with dental instruments and a carpenter's assistance, every clue deliberately positioned. She confessed to an adviser, "I found myself constantly tempted to add more clues and details…stop me when I go too far". In 1931 she endowed Harvard with $250,000 to establish legal medicine, and in 1943 New Hampshire appointed her the nation's first woman state police captain. Investigators still train on her dioramas. The privately tutored daughter of Prairie Avenue taught professional detectives how to observe.

keepsake.title: A Honeybee Hallmark
keepsake.text: An interpretive card concerning Frances Glessner Lee and her mother in 1904; a reconstruction prepared for this walk, not a historical artifact.

evidence.text: Within a few years of the wedding the Lees moved one block north into 1700 S. Prairie Avenue (demolished), one of two twin townhouses that John and Frances Glessner built for their children; their children were John Glessner Lee (1898), Frances Lee (1903) and Martha Lee (1906). 'The marriage was not a happy one and the couple divorced in 1914.'
evidence.locator: The biography of Frances Glessner Lee.

evidence.text: Fanny Glessner was born on 25 March 1878, the youngest child and only daughter, and was tutored at home. She toured Europe for fourteen months in 1896 and 1897 with her aunt Helen Macbeth, made her debut in November 1897, and on 9 February 1898 married Blewett Lee, a law partner of one of her brother George's friends.
evidence.locator: The biography of Frances Glessner Lee.

evidence.text: She married a young attorney, Blewett Lee, at 19. 'The couple had three children and at first appeared happy, but Glessner Lee eventually received a divorce.'
Mattie Williamson baked the wedding cake for Frances Glessner and Blewett Lee, married at the house on 9 February 1898.
George Glessner photographed the pair at 1700-1706 Prairie under construction in the summer of 1901, a year before the Glessner and Lee families moved in (1902).

The Daughter Who Made Things: the day, Monday 21 November 1904, the hour and the order of the walk are this jaunt's framing, chosen because the stories meet on it (three days after Arthur Caton's death, a Monday of the Reading Class, before Kimball's death in December). No visit on that day is asserted.

The Daughter Who Made Things: who is seen at each stop, where they stand, what they do and when are reconstructed. People with cards in the town play themselves; people the town has no card for (and the unnamed servants, callers and passers-by) are unnamed figures in period dress, and no likeness is claimed. No word anyone says is asserted.

George Glessner married Alice Hamlin in June 1898; their children were Elizabeth (1899), Frances (1900), John (1902) and Emily (1904). Photography was his lifelong passion, and in 1902 he was named utility manager of International Harvester.
evidence.locator: The biography of George Macbeth Glessner.

evidence.text: Their son attributed the failed marriage partly to her 'creative urge coupled with high manual dexterity—the desire to make things—which [Lee] did not share.'

In 1904 Frances Glessner set up a workbench in the basement of Glessner House and began producing simple and elegant objects; her pieces bear her hallmark, 'a G encircling a honeybee', for her bee keeping. She studied with Annibale Fogliata, a master jewelry craftsman of Hull House, and Madeline Yale Wynne, a noted Chicago silversmith.
evidence.locator: The biography of Frances Macbeth Glessner.

evidence.text: Frances Macbeth Glessner kept a journal from 1879, and in 1904 set up a silversmith's workbench in the basement of the house; she also kept bees.
evidence.locator: The biography of Frances Macbeth Glessner.

evidence.text: Sarah Frances Macbeth was born on 1 January 1848 in Urbana, Ohio, and married John Glessner on 7 December 1870.
evidence.locator: The biography of Frances Macbeth Glessner.

evidence.text: Passers-by remarked on the narrow windows in the north side along 18th Street, just enough to light the narrow corridors, not realizing that on the courtyard side Richardson had put generous windows.

In 1931 Frances Glessner Lee gave $250,000 to Harvard to create a chair in legal medicine; in 1943 New Hampshire appointed her State Police Captain, the first woman state police captain in the country. Her twenty miniature crime scenes, the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, became the teaching tool of the Seminars in Homicide Investigation, and Erle Stanley Gardner dedicated a Perry Mason novel to her. She died at The Rocks on 27 January 1962.
evidence.locator: The biography of Frances Glessner Lee.

evidence.text: The Nutshells were built at one inch to a foot with dental tools and a carpenter's help; she wrote to an adviser, 'I found myself constantly tempted to add more clues and details…stop me when I go too far.'
Frances Glessner Lee, the Glessners' daughter, later built eighteen miniature crime-scene dioramas, the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, still used in training investigators.
